6.120.m:
he has bathed at all pilgrimage places, he has been initiated in all sacrifices, / who performs an ablution with the waters of the Śālagrāma stone.

In heaven, on earth, and in the underworld there are indeed stones, O Guha, / but there is none, none equal to the rock of the Śālagrāma stone.

In this human world so hard to obtain, fruitful is the life of him / who gives with devotion a hundred prasthas of sesame day after day:

he attains that same fruit from the worship of the Śālagrāma stone. / A leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, a root, and a blade of dūrvā grass

offered upon a Śālagrāma stone becomes equal to Mount Meru. / Even someone without ritual knowledge, devoid of rites and mantras,

who bears marks of the discus on his arms, attains the complete fruit stated in the scriptures. / What was seen by me formerly in Keśava, which destroys distress,

all that I shall tell out of affection for you, O child: / 'Where do you live, O Viṣṇu? What is your base? What is your support?

Or how are you pleased, O God? Tell me all that.' / The blessed Kṛṣṇa said: / 'I constantly dwell, O Śambhu, in the stone originating from Śālagrāma.

Hear my names corresponding to that very stone marked with the chariot wheel: / If on the level entry area a discus is seen without an interval, / he is to be known as Vāsudeva, white and exceedingly auspicious.'
Pradyumna, however, has a face like the sun and a blue lustre; / it has a cavity full of perforations and is elongated in form.
Aniruddha, on the other hand, has a yellowish hue, is round, and exceedingly beautiful, / marked with three lines at the aperture, having a mark like a visible lotus.
The god Nārāyaṇa is dark, with an elevated navel and wheel, / endowed with a long straight line, and accompanied by a cavity on the right.
One should know that which has an upward face, beautiful and possessing the form of Hari, / as bestowing desire, bestowing liberation, and especially bestowing wealth.
Parameṣṭhin is white in lustre, endowed with a lotus and a wheel, / having the shape of a disc and a very ample cavity on the back.
Viṣṇu is black in color, with very beautiful wheels at the base, / and a line is seen from the middle region above the aperture.
Kapila Narasiṃha has a broad wheel and is very splendid; / he is to be worshipped with celibacy, otherwise he causes obstacles.
Vārāha has a female sexual mark, and its two wheels are remembered as unequal; / resembling a sapphire, thick, three-lined from the navel, and auspicious.
That which is elongated, gold-colored, and adorned with three dots, / should be known as the stone called Matsya, bestowing the fruit of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Kūrma is likewise raised on the back, circular, and filled with wheels; / it assumes a green color and is marked with the Kaustubha gem.
Hayagrīva is horse-shaped, adorned with five lines, / filled with many dots, and has a blue form on its back.
Vaikuṇṭha has unbroken parts, a single wheel, and a flag; / above the aperture there is a line shaped like a guñjā berry, very beautiful.
The god Śrīdhara is marked with a garland of forest flowers, / shaped like a kadamba flower, and adorned with five lines.
Vāmana is declared to be round and also short, / resembling a flax flower and adorned all around with a dot.
Then the god Sudarśana is dark in color and of great splendour, / with a mace and a wheel on the left side, and a line on the right.
Dāmodara is thick, with a wheel placed in the middle, / having the hue of dūrvā grass, a narrow aperture, and yellow lines.
Ananta is of variegated color, marked with various coils, / having many forms, broken, and bestowing the fruit of all desires.
He whose face is seen above in all the intermediate directions and directions / should be known as Puruṣottama, bestowing the fruit of enjoyment and liberation.
A liṅga arising from a Śālagrāma stone is seen on the peak; / the god Yogeśvara, to whom it belongs, removes the sin of killing a brahmin.
Padmanābha is reddish, with a lotus joined to its mouth; / from the constant worship of him, even a poor man becomes a lord.
One should point out the golden-bodied one marked with wheels, a net of rays, / abundant with lines of gold, and radiant with the lustre of crystal.
A very smooth [stone] brings accomplishment, a black one gives fame, / a pale one burns away sins, and a yellow one bestows the fruit of sons.
A blue one grants fortune, a red one causes disease, / a rough one produces agitation, and a crooked one leads to poverty.
[With] one [wheel] it is known as Sudarśana; with two, Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa; / one should know that with a third it is Acyuta, and with a fourth, Janārdana;
with a fifth, Vāsudeva; and with a sixth, Pradyumna; / with a seventh, Saṃkarṣaṇa; and with an eighth, Puruṣottama;
with a ninth, Navavyūha; and with a tenth, of that nature; / with an eleventh, Aniruddha; and with a twelve, of twelvefold nature.
Above that, wheels are seen on the stone named Ananta. / No fault is incurred if a Śālagrāma is broken, chipped, or fractured.
Whatever form is dear to a person, that one should worship with effort. / One who carries the lord of stones on his shoulder along the road—
all the three worlds, both moving and unmoving, become subject to him. / Wherever a Śālagrāma stone is, there Hari is present.
Giving, chanting, and bathing there are a hundred times greater than at Vārāṇasī, / at Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, Naimiṣa, and Puṣkara.
There the merit is ten-million-fold, bearing great fruit as at Vārāṇasī. / Whatever sin a man commits, such as killing a brahmin,
the worship of the Śālagrāma stone burns it all away quickly. / Where the god who arises from Śālagrāma is, there is the one who arises from Dvārakā;
where there is the confluence of both, liberation is there beyond doubt. / By students, householders, forest-dwellers, and mendicants
the food offering of Viṣṇu is to be consumed; no hesitation should be made here. / In its worship there are no mantras, no recitation, and no mental contemplation;
there is no praise and no formal conduct in the worship of the Śālagrāma stone. / But having made a svastika with respect in front of a Śālagrāma stone,
especially in Kārtika, one purifies up to the seventh generation of one's family. / Whoever makes even an atom-sized maṇḍala in front of Keśava
with clay and mineral pigments, dwells in heaven for ten million kalpas. / But he who tends the agnihotra for a full year
and one who makes a svastika in Kārtika—these are equal, there is no doubt. / In the case of approaching a forbidden woman and eating forbidden food,
that sin goes to destruction upon adorning the house of Hari. / The woman who daily makes a maṇḍala in front of Keśava / never suffers widowhood for seven births.

6.121.m: Whoever, having taken shelter under the shade of an āmalakī tree, offers a funeral cake, O Guha, / their ancestors attain liberation through the grace of Mādhava.
The man who bears a myrobalan fruit on his head, hands, mouth, / and body, O child, is adorned with myrobalan fruit.
A man whose diet consists of myrobalan fruit becomes Nārāyaṇa. / Whatever Vaiṣṇava in the world bears a myrobalan fruit, O Guha,
becomes dear to the gods, to say nothing of mortals. / One should not abandon a tulasī garland, and especially a garland of myrobalan.
For as long as a myrobalan garland rests on a man's neck, / so long does Keśava abide in his body.
Myrobalan, fruit, tulasī, and clay originating from Dvārakā— / fruitful is the life of him in whose house this triad exists.
For as many days as a man bears a myrobalan garland in the Kali age, / for that many thousands of yugas he will have an abode in Vaikuṇṭha.
He who wears a pair of garlands produced from myrobalan and tulasī, / wearing it on the neck region, dwells in heaven for ten million kalpas.
Restraining the collection of senses, whatever mortal performs / worship of the Śālagrāma stone with devotion, [obtains] with every flower the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Just as Viṣṇu is among the gods, so is tulasī among the flowers; / he who worships the god whose banner is Garuḍa daily with tulasī,
freed from the sorrows of birth, old age, and diseases, shall attain liberation. / He by whom Viṣṇu is worshipped with a tulasī garland in Kārtika—
Śauri distinctly wipes away the garland made of Yama's letters for him. / White sandalwood with camphor, agarwood, and saffron,
the ketakī flower, and the gift of a lamp are always dear to Keśava. / By whom a ketakī flower is offered in Kārtika in the Kali yuga,
and the gift of a lamp, O Mahāsena, delivers a hundred ancestral lines. / Lotuses, tulasī, ketakī, and the flower of the sage...

And in Kārttika on the very days of the gift of a lamp, [the devotee] who, on the fifth,
makes a flower-pavilion with a garland of ketakī flowers in Kārttika,

for Keśava, O child, his dwelling is in heaven.
When Garuḍa's banner-bearer is worshipped with a ketakī flower alone,

Madhusūdana becomes highly pleased for a thousand years.
Having worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa with flowers derived from ketakī,

he goes to that auspicious, meritorious abode of Keśava, O Guha.
When Madhu and Mādhava have arrived, having also worshipped the lord of gods with damanaka,

O best of sages, he obtains the fruit resulting from worship.
Whoever worships the god Janārdana with agasti flowers,

by the sight of him, O brahmin, the fire of hell is destroyed.
Hari, pleased by austerity, does not do that, O brahmin sage,

which he does when adorned with agasti flowers, O Mahāsena.
Leaving aside all flowers, whoever worships Keśava with an agasti flower

with devotion in Kārttika, obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Whoever offers Janārdana a garland made of agasti flowers,

even the lord of the gods, O best of sages, recounts his good deeds.
Whatever fruit is obtained by the donation of ten thousand cows, O Guha,

one obtains that fruit in Kārttika with even a single agasti flower.
Just as Hari is pleased with the Kaustubha and with the forest-garland,
And likewise Hari is delighted in Kārttika with a tulasī leaf. / Sūta said: / Seeing Kumāra bowed with humility and intent upon devotion,
the blessed Lord Mahādeva, who has a bull on his banner, spoke again: / Īśvara said: / Hear the glorification of the lamp in Kārttika, O rider of the peacock!

Surrounded by the hosts of ancestors, the ancestors always wish:
'May there be born in our family a good son devoted to his ancestors,'

who pleases Keśava by the gift of a lamp in Kārttika.
He whose lamp burns with ghee or with sesame oil,

O commander of the army, what need has he of a horse sacrifice?
By him all sacrifices have been performed; by him immersion in sacred fords has been made,

by whom the gift of a lamp was made before Keśava in Kārttika,
especially during the dark fortnight, for five days, O son.

Whoever gives a lamp on those meritorious [days], obtains imperishable [merit].
A female mouse, by trimming a lamp offered by others on the eleventh day,

attained the hard-to-reach human state and reached the supreme goal.
Even a hunter, having worshipped Maheśvara on the fourteenth,

without food, attained the supreme state and went to the world of Viṣṇu.
A vaiśya woman, having relit a lamp offered by others at the refuge of an outcaste,

became purified as Līlāvatī and went to imperishable heaven.
A certain cowherd, seeing the worship of the bow-wielder on the new-moon day,

and saying 'Victory!' repeatedly, became a sovereign over kings.
Therefore, lamps should be given at night when the sun has set,

in homes, in all cattle-pens, and in all sanctuaries,
in temples of the gods, in cremation grounds, and at lakes,

with ghee and the like for auspiciousness, during as many as five days.
Whatever ancestors are sinners whose offerings of rice-balls and water have ceased,
even they go to supreme liberation through the merit of the gift of a lamp."
